ety.text: Originally northern dialectal, from Scots pet (“an animal that has been tamed and is kept as a pet; a darling or favourite; a petted or spoiled child”), probably from Scottish Gaelic peata (“pet, tamed animal, spoiled child”), from Middle Irish petta, peta (“pet, lap-dog”), of uncertain origin, possibly from a pre-Indo-European substrate. Compare also peat (“pet, darling, woman”), which is likely not related. The verb is derived from the noun.
Clipping of petulance.
Clipping of petal.

senses.d: An animal kept as a companion or otherwise for pleasure, rather than for some practical benefit or use.
ex: family pet, pet cat, pet dog, pet store
My dog Fido has been a loyal pet for ten years.

senses.d: Something kept as a companion, including inanimate objects.
ex: pet plant, pet rock
Papyrus: This is my brother's pet rock. He always forgets to feed it. As usual, I have to take responsibility.

senses.d: One who is excessively loyal to a superior and receives preferential treatment.

ex: the love of cronies, pets, and favourites

senses.d: To stroke or fondle (an animal).
ex: I really love to pet cute puppies.

senses.d: To stroke or fondle (another person) amorously.
ex: We started petting each other the moment we were alone.
So we kissed + petted for about 15 mins. + he still wasn't hard, altho he acted like he was enjoying himself.

senses.d: To keep or treat (an animal) as a pet.

The adjective is derived from Middle English peti, pety (“little, small; minor”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman petit, Middle French petit, and Old French peti, petit, pitet (“young; little, small; inferior; insignificant”) (modern French petit), ultimately of imitative origin. It is no longer thought that the word is derived from Celtic. Doublet of petit and petite. The noun is derived from the adjective.

ex: a petty fault    petty squabbles
His birth, perhaps, ſome petty Village hides, / And ſets his Cradle out of Fortune's way: […]

senses.d: Of persons or their behaviour: marked by or reflective of undesirably limited interests, sympathies, or views; begrudging, selfish, small-minded; also, preoccupied with subjects having little or no importance and not mindful of broader concerns.
ex: Such literature may well be anathema to those who are too docile and petty for their own good.
That corporation is only slightly pettier than they are greedy, and they are overdue to reap the consequences.

senses.d: Inclined to cause frustration or annoyance to others out of spite over minor grievances; extremely vindictive.

Unknown. Attested from the 18th century. The Canting Academy defines peeter as “A portmantle”; Green’s Dictionary of Slang list a variety of uses for peter – including trunk or portmanteau – in thieves’ cant in Britain, Australia, New Zealand, and the United States.
